items.title: Wales fightback not enough as Australia edge thriller thanks to Gordon
items.desc:
• Wales 26-29 Australia

  • Wales to face Japan in ninth-place final

One step at a time. Historic victories are one thing, but the boring need to back up such a win proved beyond Wales. Cardiff was rocking. A few thousand short of capacity the stadium may have been, but 66,000 rocked it as of yore. Wales’s young side could not quite respond.

This was a reverse of last weekend’s win against New Zealand. In the first half, in particular, Wales’s dominance was all but total, but like the All Blacks, they just could not make it tell. Australia had the lead at the break and in a more open second half they proved just as deadly. Thus they claim their place in the fifth-place final at Twickenham, where they will face Ireland on Friday night. Wales must make do with a ninth-placed final against Japan on Saturday.

items.title: England hail ‘inspirational’ Lewis Moody after thrashing New Zealand
items.desc:
• Former captain, who has MND, was on pitch for haka

  • ‘Players jumped at the opportunity to support him’

England’s players have hailed the former national captain Lewis Moody as their chief source of inspiration after the record-breaking 37-12 Twickenham drubbing of New Zealand. Moody, who has motor neurone disease, joined the home side on the pitch for the pre-match haka and the current skipper, Maro Itoje, said his presence helped to fuel their outstanding performance.

Never in their distinguished history have the All Blacks lost by a wider margin to northern-hemisphere opposition and Itoje suggested a desire to underline their support for Moody and his family had been a significant motivation. “Lewis is such an inspirational man,” said Itoje, after his side’s fifth consecutive Test victory. “He was an inspirational player, too, and the players jumped at the opportunity to support him. He came to spend some time with us yesterday, presented us our shirts for the game and addressed us. There’s no doubt that him joining us for the haka and spending time with us gave us an extra lift today.”

items.title: England’s strength in depth finally comes together in landmark victory over All Blacks | Andy Bull
items.desc:
Record-breaking win suggests Steve Borthwick’s side are realising their enormous potential at last

Something’s coming. Oh yes. They will be able to hear its approaching footsteps in Edinburgh and Dublin and Paris and Cardiff, the tremors will ripple through Johannesburg and Sydney all the way to Auckland, where they will finally arrive sometime when the New Zealand public wakes up to find out all about what happened to their team here at Twickenham. After years of being oh so ordinary, England are on their way at long last to looking like the sort of team their depth of talent and wealth of resources has always suggested they ought to be.

When they beat Australia, everyone said how woeful the Wallabies were, when they thrashed Japan, all the talk was about how far the Brave Blossoms had fallen, but there are no caveats when you beat New Zealand like this. There’s no such thing as an easy win against the All Blacks. And no such thing, either, as a bad All Blacks team, even if this one’s a long way short of their best. It was a record victory, the 25-point margin eight more than England managed to win by in their famous victory here in 2012. Honestly, it could, maybe should, have been by more. England had enough opportunities to score twice as many.

Snapping a four-game losing streak, the Wallabies edged Wales in a performance that showed progress under Les Kiss

The Wallabies had one per cent possession in the final ten minutes and still hung on to win. Those one percenters are exactly what Les Kiss is trying to rebuild after two blowout defeats to New Zealand, a bashing by England and a brutal beatdown by Scotland last week. Now, after entering the Dragon’s lair and silencing 75,000 Welsh, the rediscovery of such tiny tantalising margins is inching Australia back to their best

By defeating Wales 26-29, the Wallabies have snapped their four-match losing streak and snatched their first win in eight northern hemisphere Tests to stay alive in the Nations Championship. Best of all, they did the little things that produce big results. This win has roused their self belief, restored the composure and creativity they had lost in attack, and given them a sniff of finishing a rollercoaster season on a high.

items.title: Kildunne returns to haunt Harlequins as Bristol get PWR season off to a flyer
items.desc:
• Harlequins 21-48 Bristol

  • Full-back marks debut with two tries against former club

As women’s rugby grows, more scrutiny will follow and Ellie Kildunne has felt that over the past few months. Her performances have been put under a microscope after being dropped to the bench in England’s final two WXV matches in October, but she silenced her critics with a stellar and trademark performance in her club debut for Bristol. The full-back did it under significant pressure, too, as she returned to the Stoop five months after her shock exit from Harlequins and helped Bristol beat her former side in their Premiership Women’s Rugby opener.

The Bristol head coach, Scott Lawson, had thrown his full backing behind Kildunne in the buildup, saying that being at the West Country club would “bring the best” out of the 27-year-old and if her debut is anything to go by he will be proved right. The World Cup winner not only scored two tries but was also a linchpin in Bristol’s attack. Her attacking prowess and gamechanging reputation was felt among her former teammates as she drew multiple players to her whenever she had the ball, meaning the wings on her outside had a lot more joy. The back three looked formidable with both wings, Reneeqa Bonner and Millie David, also scoring two tries apiece.

items.title: Steve Borthwick hits rewind button to inspire England’s flying starts
items.desc:
The head coach said he has watched videos from Eddie Jones’ time in charge to help England start matches strongly

Ellis Genge was so fired up by England’s powerful response to the haka on Saturday he stripped off his anthem jacket in the aftermath, completely forgetting he was not starting. Ollie Chessum told Lewis Moody, who had been invited to stand at the point of England’s V formation, “we are going long left, stay on the field and chase the kick-off”. And according to Ben Earl, who would still be out on the Twickenham turf carrying through traffic if he could, some players were so inspired by Moody’s speech the night before they could not sleep.

Against that emotional backdrop, it is small wonder England flew out of the blocks against the All Blacks. Steve Borthwick has spoken a lot about “bringing the fire” recently and on Saturday they torched the place, riding the emotional wave that Moody’s presence inspired from Henry Slade’s fourth-minute try, through to a record victory against New Zealand.

Whatever still awaits on the inaugural Nations Championship finals weekend, it has been a richly enjoyable few weeks for both diehard fans and floating voters, topped off by more seismic results and overflowing emotions in London and Dublin on Saturday.

Those flocking to Twickenham had their money’s worth even before the game started, as Lewis Moody, fighting the good fight against motor neurone disease, stood shoulder to shoulder with England’s players as they faced up to the All Blacks’ haka.
